# Week 4, Day 3.1 — Prerequisites check

**No new TypeScript today.** Everything you need is an options object and a number.

| You'll use | Taught in |
|---|---|
| Objects as options (`{ mode: "parallel" }`) | [week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1) |
| Numeric separators (`60_000`) | [week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1) |
| Arrow functions | [week3/day2_1](/learn/w3/d2/p1) |

Today builds directly on two earlier days — [week3/day1_2](/learn/w3/d1/p2) (timeouts) and
[week3/day5_2](/learn/w3/d5/p2) (workers and parallelism). If either is hazy, skim it first:
today is about moving those same settings to a smaller scope.

**Next:** [Day 3.2 — Changing settings without disturbing your team](/learn/w4/d3/p2)

# Week 4, Day 3.2 — Changing settings without disturbing your team

You need one test to run in parallel, or one test to wait longer. Editing
`playwright.config.ts` gets you there — and changes the behaviour of every test your colleagues
own. By the end of this lesson you can make the change in the smallest possible place.

> **Mode: test-runner.** This part is about running specs with the Playwright test runner. The studio editor runs library code, so follow these along in your own checkout.

## The problem with editing the shared config

A config change is a change to everyone's suite:

| You want | If you edit the config | Cost to the team |
|---|---|---|
| one group to run in parallel | `fullyParallel: true` | dependent tests elsewhere start failing |
| one slow test to wait longer | `timeout: 80_000` | *every* failure now takes 80s to report |
| to try three workers | `workers: 3` | someone's serial suite breaks |

None of these are hypothetical. And nobody remembers to change them back, so a temporary
experiment becomes the team's permanent default.

Playwright's answer is that most of these settings can also be set **in the spec**, where they
affect only what you own.

## Three scopes, smallest first

| Scope | How | Affects |
|---|---|---|
| One assertion | `expect(x).toBeVisible({ timeout: 9_000 })` | that one check |
| One test | `test.setTimeout(60_000)` / `test.slow()` | that one test |
| One `describe` group | `test.describe.configure({ mode: "parallel" })` | that group |
| Everything | the config file | **everyone** |

Pick the narrowest row that solves your problem. That's the whole of today.

## Example 1 — parallel for one group only

**Objective:** run three tests concurrently without touching `fullyParallel`.

`test.describe.configure()` goes inside the group. `mode: "parallel"` lets its tests run at the
same time; `mode: "serial"` forces them in order — which is what
[week3/day2_2](/learn/w3/d2/p2) used for dependent tests.

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week4/generated/day3-script-level.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `7 passed`.

Two groups, two different policies, one file. The first is `mode: "parallel"`; the second isn't,
so it uses whatever the config says. Neither changed the config.

**The precondition for parallel is independence.** Those three tests each sign in on their own
`page` and share nothing. Mark a dependent group parallel and you get failures that look random —
that's the same lesson as week3, from the other direction.

## Example 2 — a longer budget for one test

`test.setTimeout()` is the first line inside the test body. It replaces the budget for that test
only.

**Expected:** four lines, narrowest scope first.

`test.slow()` is worth knowing: it multiplies the configured timeout by three rather than naming
a number. That keeps working when the config changes, whereas a hardcoded `60_000` quietly stops
being three times the default.

The spec above proves the isolation — one test raises its budget to 60s, and the next test
asserts its own budget is still **below** 60s. The override didn't leak.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## What you cannot move into the spec

There is no `test.setExpectTimeout()`. The auto-retrying assertion deadline is either:

- a config value — `expect: { timeout: 8_000 }`, or
- an option on the individual assertion — `toBeVisible({ timeout: 9_000 })`

And `test.setTimeout()` does **not** touch it. Raise the test budget to 45 seconds and an
assertion still gives up after its own 5 — which produces the confusing situation where a test
with a generous timeout fails in five seconds.

| Setting | Config | Per test | Per assertion |
|---|---|---|---|
| test/action timeout | yes | **yes** | — |
| expect timeout | yes | **no** | **yes** |
| parallel mode | yes | **yes** (per describe) | — |
| workers | yes | **no** | — |
| retries | yes | no (per describe: `retries`) | — |

Workers are the other one people expect to be per-spec and aren't: a worker is an OS process, so
it's decided before your file is even loaded.

## Best practices

- **Narrowest scope that works.** Assertion, then test, then group, then config.
- **`test.slow()` over a hardcoded number** when you just mean "this one is heavy".
- **Only mark a group parallel if its tests are genuinely independent.**
- **Config changes get discussed**, because they're changes to other people's suites.
- **Never leave an experiment in the config.** If it must go there, it needs a comment saying why.

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Assertion fails in 5s despite `setTimeout(45_000)` | expect has its own deadline | pass `{ timeout }` to the assertion |
| Parallel group fails randomly | its tests aren't independent | `mode: "serial"`, or make them independent |
| `test.setTimeout` seems ignored | called outside the test body | first line *inside* the test |
| Colleague's suite broke after your push | you edited the shared config | move it into your spec |
| `workers` in a spec does nothing | it's process-level | set it in the config or on the CLI |

**Next:** [Day 3.3](/learn/w4/d3/p3) — which knob belongs where, on a real team.

# Week 4, Day 3.3 — Where settings belong on a real team

Same overrides as [Day 3.2](/learn/w4/d3/p2). No new API. The question is which knob belongs in the
repo, which belongs in a spec, and which belongs on the command line.

## Three homes, three lifetimes

| Home | Lifetime | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Command line** | one run | `--headed`, `--workers=1`, `--repeat-each`, `--debug` |
| **Spec file** | as long as that test exists | this group is parallel; this test is slow |
| **Config** | forever, for everyone | baseURL, reporters, trace policy, the browser matrix |

The test for the config is simple: **would every current and future teammate want this?** A
reporter, yes. Your 80-second timeout because one screen is slow today, no.

**Expected:** eight lines, each naming a home.

Read the CLI rows together: they are all **temporary by construction**. Nothing to remember to
remove, nothing to review, nothing that can leak into someone else's run. That's why the command
line is the right home for anything you're only doing today.

## The escape hatch that becomes technical debt

A per-test override is a small, local, documented decision — or an undocumented workaround that
outlives everyone who understood it. The difference is one comment:

```ts
// Statement generation calls a third-party PDF service; 45s is its p99.
// Ticket PERF-284 tracks getting this under 10s.
test.setTimeout(45_000);
```

versus:

```ts
test.setTimeout(45_000);
```

The second one will still be there in three years, and nobody will dare remove it because nobody
knows what breaks. Every override worth keeping is worth one line of why.

## What a reviewer checks

- **Is this the narrowest scope** that solves the problem?
- **Does a config change belong to everyone**, or is it one person's workaround?
- **Does each override carry a reason** — ideally a ticket?
- **Is a parallel group actually independent?**
- **Nothing temporary committed** — no `--headed` equivalent, no `slowMo`, no stray `only`.

**Next:** [Day 3.4](/learn/w4/d3/p4) — your turn.

# Week 4, Day 3.4 — Practice

Three problems. No answer key.

App: `https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/`. Do not edit the root
`playwright.config.ts` in any of these — that constraint *is* the exercise.

> Stuck past twenty minutes? Back to [Day 3.2](/learn/w4/d3/p2).

## When you're done

**The deletion check from Problem 3 is worth running on real suites too.** Overrides accumulate
because adding one is easy and removing one feels risky. Deleting them and watching what actually
fails converts a guess into evidence.

**Next:** [Day 4.1](/learn/w4/d4/p1) — elements you can see but cannot reach.

problems.statement:
**Build.** Prove an override is local.

1. A `describe` with two tests, the first raising its own timeout with `test.setTimeout`
2. In the second test, assert that **its** timeout is still the config default
3. Print both values so you can see them

**Check yourself.** Both pass, and the printed numbers differ. If they match, the override
leaked — or you called `setTimeout` outside a test body.

> **Hint** — `test.info().timeout` tells you the current test's budget.

**Build.** The same four tests under two different policies, timed.

1. A `describe` marked `mode: "serial"` with four independent dashboard tests
2. A second `describe` marked `mode: "parallel"` with the same four tests
3. Run the file and record each group's duration

**Check yourself.** The parallel group is faster. State both numbers, then answer: what would
happen to the parallel group if those four tests shared one `page` via `beforeAll`?

> **Hint** — `--reporter=list` prints per-test durations. The second question has a specific
> failure mode, not just "it would be slower".

**Build.** A spec that needs three different scopes, and justify each.

Write four tests against the banking app where:

1. One needs a longer **assertion** deadline (and nothing else)
2. One needs a longer **test** budget
3. One is marked `test.slow()` rather than given a number
4. One needs no override at all

Each override carries a comment saying **why** and what would make it removable.

**Where.** A spec in `week4/generated/`.

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- **No edit to the root `playwright.config.ts`**
- **No `waitForTimeout`**
- Every test passes **run on its own**

Then answer in a comment: *which of your four overrides is most likely to still exist in two
years, and is that a good thing?*

**Check yourself.** Passes together and individually. Then delete all four overrides and run
again — how many tests fail? If the answer is zero, none of them were needed, which is itself the
finding.

> **Hint** — that deletion check is the real exercise. An override that changes nothing is noise
> a future reader has to reason about.
